speechtext: The Prime Minister did not deal at all with the first part of the question which pertained to these people having the right which was laid down in the 1963 guidelines by then Prime Minister Pearson and subsequently endorsed by the present Prime Minister in 1969 to be informed that their reliability was in question. subsubtopic: NOTIFICATION OF PEOPLE WHOSE NAMES ON BLACKLIST AND REMOVAL OF NOTATION OF BLACKLISTING FROM PERSONAL FILES
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. The point of my previous answer was that in no way did this information which was collected by the police adversely affect the careers of these people. Mr. Pearson's guidelines, my own and those of this government, state that if security information collected by police agencies in some way adversely affects the career of any person, that person should be entitled to refute the information, discuss it, contradict it and so on. I repeat that this circumstance did not arise. I believe that is the answer the Acting Prime Minister gave yesterday.
What in fact happened is a very simple sequence of events. The police select whatever information comes their way which might have to do with the security of this country. Their role is to take it in, collect it and, I suppose, sift it and verify it. However, their role is not to act on it. When they have this information, they hand it to the Solicitor General. I presume that if the Solicitor General had done nothing about it, he would be accused today of not doing anything about information which came his way from the police about possible security lists.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I began my speech yesterday I put on the record the fact that unemployment in December, 1976, jumped to 7.5 per cent. The number of unemployed was 754,000, up from 693,000 the year before. I also put on the record some provincial unemployment figures for December of 1976. 1 do not want to repeat those figures, but I was in the middle of saying-and I will complete the sentence-that the unemployment figure in

British Columbia for December of 1976 was 92,000, an increase from the figure of 82,000 in December of 1975.
There was a sharp increase in the jobless rate for young workers in the 15 to 24 year age group. In that group 14 per cent of the eligible workers were out of work in December, and as my colleague, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), has already indicated, this is the group which will be most adversely affected by the decision incorporated in this bill to increase the number of weeks during which a person has to work before qualifying for unemployment insurance, from eight weeks to twelve weeks.
The minister and some hon. members of the official opposition implied that there are jobs for many of the unemployed, both those who have been counted and the thousands who have not been counted. We know from the questions which were asked about a week ago by members of the New Democratic Party and by members of the Conservative party from the maritime provinces that the figures which I have quoted are not the real unemployment figures. Those figures do not take into account thousands of people, especially in slow growth areas like the Atlantic provinces and like the interlake area of Manitoba, where the rate is probably twice as high as the official rate because so many people have simply given up hope of finding work even if they look for it. I think it was the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who estimated that in Newfoundland the real rate of unemployment is probably not the 14.5 per cent Statistics Canada gives us but probably 30 per cent.
If we are going to start making things tougher, as a number of hon. members of the Conservative party suggested yesterday we should, if we are going to police the unemployment insurance system more actively, if we are going to put more restrictions on people qualifying, and if we are going to cut off people who do not meet certain standards, it seems obvious to me that we do that because we believe that there are many jobs which can be filled by people who are unemployed, people who are drawing unemployment insurance benefits, and people on welfare who simply do not want to look for those jobs.
Statistics Canada tells us not only the number of people who are unemployed but also the number of job vacancies in this country, and according to information Statistics Canada released just a few days ago, in the fourth quarter of 1976 the number of full time, part time or casual labour job vacancies decreased from 62,300 for the same period in 1975 to 41,700 in 1976. In other words, if every one of the almost 42,000 job vacancies was filled, there would still be over 710,000 people unemployed.
If we look at the provincial breakdown for job vacancies, we can get an understanding of what is happening in this country. In Alberta, where there is almost full employment and little unemployment, and people can afford to quit one job in order to look for another, there are 13 job vacancies for every 1,000 people. In Saskatchewan, where employment is at relatively high levels and where there is not much unemployment, there are eight job vacancies for every 1,000 people. But in Nova Scotia there are two job vacancies for every 1,000 people.
February 2, 1977

Therefore it is not surprising that people in Nova Scotia do not quit their jobs easily, do not leave their jobs unless they have other jobs waiting.
I am not surprised that many in Canada are under the mistaken impression that thousands of our unemployed could find jobs if only they wanted them badly enough. I am not surprised that some members of the official opposition think that, although I should expect members from the Atlantic provinces, where there is heavy unemployment, to know better. But I find it most disturbing that senior officials of the Department of Manpower and Immigration do not agree with Statistics Canada figures relating to unemployment and job vacancies.
I want to put on record the views of the Assistant Deputy Minister of Manpower, Mr. Harry Hodder, as expressed in the Toronto Star on December 10, 1976. I do not often raise in this House the views of senior civil servants; but when a senior civil servant grants an interview or makes a speech which is reported in a newspaper, I think it is quite proper to comment and put his views, as expressed in the newspaper article, on record. I hope the minister is listening because the point is important. Mr. Hodder's views, as expressed in that newspaper article, part of which I shall quote in a moment, show an inexcusable contempt for people. The expression of such views on the part of a public servant is indefensible, and I question whether he should be employed as a public servant.
The headline over the story in the Toronto Star reads, "50,000 'vagrants' to be cut off unemployment." The article quotes Mr. Hodder, who deals with the 50,000 people who will be cut off from unemployment insurance under the new regulations which will require a person to work for 12 weeks instead of eight weeks before collecting unemployment insurance. The first part of the article is in quotation marks. Mr. Hodder is quoted as saying this;
'They are mostly young people, moving in and out of the labour force and using unemployment insurance to fatten their income'...
The next part of the article I shall quote paraphrases Mr. Hodder's views, as follows:
Government studies estimate the 50,000 claimants eliminated under the bill can easily find work if they want to.
The studies estimate that it is unlikely that more than 2 per cent or 3 per cent of them would be forced to seek welfare.
Part of the next paragraph is in direct quotation marks and reads:
'The fact is, a very small proportion of them really need unemployment insurance benefits. They've been getting money for jam'...
Later, the article goes on to say this:
Hodder, who estimates the experiment might cost $5 million in the first year, says: it's better than having them lying in bed drinking beer.'
I suggest that a deputy minister earning probably more than $40,000 a year-

Not allegedly; they are in quotation marks. I am sure the assistant deputy minister saw that story, and if he was misquoted he would have made his complaints to the newspaper. I have quoted an article which appeared more than six weeks ago. I think I have every right to quote it. If the assistant deputy minister was misquoted, as the minister suggests or alleges, it was his job, not mine, to take that question up with the newspaper. I merely say that what he is quoted as saying is in line with the minister's thinking, as expressed yesterday. The minister may shake his head, but I suggest that lam correct.
We face the prospect of more unemployment in this country than at any time since World War II. The projections of government organizations, academics, banks and insurance companies show that unemployment will be worse in 1977 than it was in 1976. I could spend a couple of hours reading such dismal reports into the record.
I shall quote one more newspaper story, written by Wayne Cheveldayoff in the Globe and Mail of January 11, 1977. Dealing with the statistics issued by various economic organizations, he said:
Economic forecasters expect real gross national product (excluding inflation) to advance by about 3.5 per cent this year-a rate of growth that is significantly below the long run potential rate and down from last year's gain of 5 per cent...
Despite the expected stimulus, 1977, as the second year of recovery from the 1974-75 recession, will show slower growth in all components of GNP (excluding housing construction and business capital investment) than the average for the past five economic recoveries ... The jobless number will exceed 850,000, while job vacancies remain under 100,000.
That is precisely what I said earlier. Mr. Cheveldayoff in his article estimated that the unemployment rate for all 1977 will fluctuate between 7.5 per cent and 8 per cent. We say that kind of unemployment is unnecessary. We do not think the country can afford that kind of unemployment. We do not think it is necessary to pay out as much in unemployment

insurance and welfare as we have paid out in recent years. My party is not alone in putting forth this opinion. That is also the opinion of the former head of the Economic Council, Arthur Smith.
A number of economists in governments, universities, and business have been calling on the government to stimulate the economy and follow the example set by President Carter. He has proposed a two-year program, to which Congress will undoubtedly agree, calling for the expenditure of $31 billion. Half that amount will be used for job creation; the other half will make its impact felt in the form of tax cuts, to stimulate the economy. We do not have anything like that being proposed for this country by this government.
I wish to give one example of what unemployment has caused us. An article by Don McGillivray appeared in the January 12 edition of the Montreal Gazette. He calculated what unemployment has done to this country. He stated that last year 9,572,000 Canadians who worked produced about $180 billion worth of goods and services, the gross national product. That works out to $18,800 for the average employed Canadian. However, 736,000 Canadians were unemployed. That is the number averaged over the whole year who were officially out of work and seeking jobs.
He pointed out that, until a few years ago, the Economic Council calculated that full employment would be reached when we had only 3 per cent unemployed. He does not agree. He said that in recent years the Economic Council increased the rate of unemployment which they believed would represent full employment to 4'/2 per cent. He stated that even if you take that figure there were 286,000 Canadians in 1976 who should have been working but were in fact unemployed.
Mr. McGillivray pointed out that if you assume that these are the least productive people, and if you cut in half the $18,000 average which was produced by each Canadian citizen who was employed, which would be about $9,000, you come to a figure of $2.5 billion in lost employment which we had in this country because of the existing unemployment.
The government has not taken the problem of unemployment at all seriously. It has paid little more than lip service with regard to the objective of achieving full employment. The LIP, LEAP and OFY programs have not been serious instruments in a broad, consistent attack on unemployment.
There is no iron law which states we cannot reduce unemployment to 3 per cent. Other countries have done it. France, Japan, Sweden and Germany had unemployment of less than 2 per cent in the ten year period 1962 to 1973 while our unemployment in that period averaged over 5 per cent. That level of unemployment is neither natural nor acceptable.
We have to take whatever steps are necessary to achieve full employment. The government is not doing that. Instead of aiming for full employment, as I said last night, there have been massive expenditures for manpower training for jobs which simply do not exist. They have not existed in the years we have had manpower training, they do not exist today, and

are not likely to exist unless the government takes a much more active role in producing jobs than it has in recent years.
As I said last night, the manpower programs we have had have been aimed in the wrong direction. I quoted a sentence or two from the study commissioned by the C. D. Howe Institute on manpower training programs by Barbara Goldman. She found that current manpower programs are heavily weighted toward training, even though the training does not match the labour job market requirements. She found the program started and stopped, not because of manpower or job needs, but because of political decisions on the part of the government. This department has consistently been wrong in the advice it has given to the government and in the kinds of programs it has offered to the public.
I want to spend a few minutes on the proposals in this bill, first with regard to job creation. The government is proposing that UIC recipients who accept work on federal government work projects will be paid out of UIC funds and will receive the greater of UIC rates or the prevailing wage rate for that job in that area. Refusal to join such a project, or quitting the job once employed, will not result in disqualification. However, working on such projects will not be considered "employment" and will not make one eligible for future UIC benefits. It sounds like a cheap way to get work done. It gets paid out of the UIC fund rather than departmental budgets, and it does not provide the worker with credits for future UIC benefits. That could create a very serious situation for people who participate in such programs.
It is interesting to compare the proposal made in 1977 with what a former minister of manpower and immigration said. That member tried to be elected to the Quebec National Assembly at the time of its recent election. This was in 1966 when the House was debating estimates for his then new department. In response to a proposal by an opposition member for job creation programs, he said and I quote:
The hon. member made a suggestion with which I basically disagree when he said we should try to find part-time work for those who draw unemployment insurance. Unemployment insurance is a type of insurance. The people who get unemployment insurance are not living on public charity. If we give start to competition between workers and those who are on unemployment insurance, 1 fear we will create an unbearable situation. Those people start working for lower salaries and will finally end up competing with regular workers. To my mind we must instead find regular employment for the people on unemployment insurance, full-time jobs that will afford them a livelihood. We must not allow them to compete against the working class.
In recent years I have usually disagreed with the then minister, but I must say that in 1966 he had a very sound, humanitarian, and realistic point of view, one with which I agreed completely.
In order to free up training funds, people eligible for UIC would be paid their training allowance, the greater of UIC or training rates, out of UIC funds, thus leaving more training money available for those who cannot qualify for UIC. Looking over Manpower's budgets from 1970-71 to 1974-75, we see that the department has spent up to 75 per cent of its annual budget on manpower training. For what purpose? To keep training the same people over and over again for jobs that do not exist. Very little is spent on job creation. This scheme is

another example of the kinds of things which should not be done.
I wish now to put on record a criticism by a provincial civil servant which I believe to be very valid. He is active and knowledgeable in the field of manpower training and education. He said, and I quote:
The manpower system in Canada has also witnessed considerable change in the past 20 years. This development has been primarily quantitative with scant attention to the interests and needs of the manpower trainees. Manpower decision makers have concentrated upon re-educating, retraining, and remolding the trainees without much attention to changing the requirements of the labour market.
My hon. friend from Nickel Belt talked about the large number of women being trained to become hairdressers in Newfoundland, probably enough to supply the entire need for hairdressers in all of Canada. I am not against hairdressers, but we can only use so many of them in this country.
The growth of the many manpower programs obscures the illogic of much of this direction. The absence of full employment often ensures training for more skilled unemployment. Differing levels of training allowances and attendance and varying recruitment systems for trainees, reinforce the standard educational systems under which universities are essentially for the children of middle and upper classes, community colleges are for the blue collar class, and adult basic education, with its related purposes courses, is for society's losers. I think that is a valid assessment of what we find in our manpower training program.
I want to talk now about one other proposal which is before us, that is, the developmental use of the unemployment insurance fund. One of the proposed sweeteners in this bill is the use of unemployment insurance funds to help create employment. These measures are supposed to be brought into play in the fall of 1977 as part of the government's push to reduce unemployment.
We have the work-sharing proposal, a scheme by which an employer who is forced to lay off part of his work force could make an agreement with the government whereby he would instead reduce the number of hours worked by everyone and the government would pay UIC benefits to everyone to make up for their drop in income. Participation in work-sharing would not affect eligibility for benefits later on. While it would be nice to prevent lay-offs, will the scheme not turn into another way to subsidize employers who claim they are forced into a lay-off? One remembers the Training in Industry program which had to be abandoned when the department found out it was simply subsidizing employers who were paying low wages. Work-sharing agreements will not be subject to appeal. The cost of this developmental use will be borne by employee-employer contributions.
When I saw that proposal, Mr. Speaker, it seemed inconceivable to me that it could have been approved by employer and employee groups which usually advise the Department of Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I took the trouble to inquire whether the matter had even been
Employment and Immigration
discussed with those people, and I was informed by a source which I believe to be reliable that this and other proposals were not even discussed with the advisory committee on unemployment insurance.
I have sometimes not agreed with all the views of my friends in the labour movement. I was not enthused, to put it mildly, by their reaction to the government's anti-inflation program, their manifesto and the call for tripartism. But how can the government expect to get the co-operation of labour or industry on basic matters such as this, in the light of present economic circumstances and the very large number of unemployed, if it does not deal in depth, if it does not deal honestly and frankly with the people who are so vitally concerned?
I am not saying that those people will necessarily agree with this or any other proposal. I am not saying that a government should not act in the absence of unanimous agreement. Governments may feel they are bound to act even if a particular group or vested interest disagrees with a program which has been proposed. But how can a government expect to get co-operation and bring in a successful program when, in a field where for 25 years or more there have been institutions such as advisory committees, questions of this kind are not even discussed?
The government is not interested, though, in what labour wants. It is not interested in what the employers want. After all, the government has experts of its own, bureaucrats.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating here one of the most difficult and complex social problems a government can face. It is not just a question of unemployment, important though that question may be, and it is not just a question of unemployment insurance, important though that program undoubtedly is. We are discussing the whole range of problems which go to create a dynamic, complex and fluid labour market, incorporating a huge annual addition of new workers and shifting with the pressures of international trade and commerce.
In such a situation no government can have a higher priority than to deal effectively with unemployment. I believe that the income earned from the dignity of work is preferable to the income which arrives in the form of an unemployment insurance cheque. And I believe that we must support and develop an employment strategy designed to create what unemployed Canadians most want and need-the dignity and personal satisfaction provided by real and worth-while jobs, not to mention an earned income higher than unemployment insurance benefits.
Although private sector employment is expected to keep growing, the number of jobs in the short term over the next year or two cannot realistically be expected to increase much faster than the number of Canadians seeking those jobs.

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Moreover, in the early 1980's, when the influx of young people seeking jobs will taper off, we may well face a situation in which the shortage becomes one of workers rather than jobs. Therefore, we must have a strategy which will provide jobs today but meet the need of tomorrow.
Our strategy must be one which will avoid massive inflation-stimulating deficits. It must not be a strategy of major monetary or fiscal stimulation, vast programs of public construction or public service expansion, or major tax cuts. These would not help to reduce inflationary forces. What we need, and what the government's employment strategy aims to achieve, is a progressive reduction of unemployment over the next five years without generating other major problems.
I believe the vast majority of Canadians want to work. And there is work to be done. But since there is no single cause underlying our rate of unemployment, there is no single solution either. There must, however, be a unified strategy, not to cure unemployment but to help keep it down, a strategy which allows us to reduce unemployment progressively over the next few years in a way consistent with the removal of wage and price controls.
Our labour market is too dynamic and the problems too complex and fluid to be able to afford a fragmented, inefficient approach to employment policy and to the organization of the labour market. That is why we are merging the UIC and the Department of Manpower and Immigration into the new commission and department of employment and immigration, and that is why the new organization must continue and strengthen the participation of business and labour in its work.
The activities of all levels of government in the labour market must also be better co-ordinated, as I think the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) was correct to point out yesterday in the course of his rambling remarks. But I might just point out in that connection that figures from the district UIC office in my own riding indicate that not more than two people would be added to the welfare rolls each week as a direct result of the increased entrance requirement. And the London district office serves not just one constituency, but three. I hope that the hon. member, therefore, was not suggesting that long consultations are necessary before the federal government should propose changes in unemployment insurance legislation which would effectively place two additional people per week on the assistance rolls in the area served by a centre as large as London, especially when the cost of that assistance is shared 50-50 with the federal government.
With a stronger institutional base, then, and with co-operation from the private sector and between governments, we can reduce our employment problems in Canada if we can plan an effective, flexible strategy. The government has such a strategy, Mr. Speaker, a strategy with three components. The first is a comprehensive job creation program squarely based on community priorities; the second consists of youth employment and employability measures, to ease the transition from school to work for young people, who make up half the unemployed;

the third is a group of selective preventive measures to reduce the loss of work and hasten a return to employment.
We all recognize that a permanent private sector job is what Canadians most want and that we must help them find it. But we must also recognize that when private sector jobs do not exist in sufficient numbers, we have an obligation, both to the unemployed themselves and to the Canadian community, to make sure that people can have work and the incomes that go with work.
From the point of view of both society and the individual concerned, work is far better than just giving people a cheque. The cost of unemployment is not just a loss of so many dollars or so much output. Much of the cost comes in failed career hopes, lost opportunities and eroded skills, in family stress, and in a growing dependency on the working members of the community.
Unemployment, therefore, is costly not only for our economy and our society, but most particularly for the worker who loses his job. Idleness brings loss of skills, loss of confidence, and erodes the worker's feeling that he participates in his community. While he may need, and has a right to income maintenance, we must be able to offer him something more. The government is now developing job creation models in which workers who are likely to be unemployed and on unemployment insurance for some months would be invited to participate in activities which have social betterment value for their communities.
We have in mind projects which would utilize many of the best features of earlier local initiatives programs, but which could be tailored more carefully to the needs of the individual-his need to spend some time in a continued job search, and his need for job counselling. The plan would allow participants to continue receiving UIC benefits, and they could receive additional support, for example, from cost of work allowances and for project overhead costs. These additional moneys would have to be voted for this purpose.
In 1977-78, the first full year of the government's five-year employment strategy, there will be an investment in the neighbourhood of $350 million over and above regular expenditures on manpower programs. And in that five-year period much of the incremental funding for the employment strategy will come from changes in the unemployment insurance legislation.
In the first full year, for instance, savings to the government from the legislative changes will be about $110 million. Future savings will be even greater. Because unemployment insurance savings will mount as unemployment declines, we can look at costs and resources averaged over five years. It is therefore expected that, if parliament approved the changes that have been proposed in the Unemployment Insurance Act, reduced government contributions to the unemployment insurance account will offset the incremental costs of this employment strategy.
Some people are repeatedly on unemployment insurance because they lack basic job skills and would benefit from occupational training or re-training. Although there is already
February 2, 1977

some integration of unemployment insurance and training allowances, the system is complex, and the training program which is entirely voluntary cannot accommodate all who need training.
Another potential developmental use of unemployment insurance is the short work week. In Europe some enterprises- enterprises which would otherwise have to lay off part of their work force-retain all workers on the job with shorter hours. Allowances are paid in respect of the difference between the hours worked and the normal work week. This sort of program requires the co-operation of company and union, but it has the great advantage of keeping people on the job and maintaining the skills of those workers during temporary business downturns.
Canada has one of the world's most efficient and comprehensive unemployment insurance programs, but it must be adapted continually in order to keep pace with changes in society and in the labour market. The proposed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act are designed, at the same time, to make that program more effective in protecting Canadian workers from the financial hardship of unemployment, without spending money which would be better allocated to employment programs.
The proposals put forward by the minister are designed to enhance motivation for work, to achieve simplicity, and to provide equity. There will be a more equitable relationship between the number of insured weeks and benefit entitlement in the initial benefit period. Greater equity will result, too, from eliminating the national unemployment rate as a trigger for extended benefits and from basing regional extended benefits entirely on regional unemployment rates. Regional rates are a better indicator of the difficulty of finding and holding employment. While the benefit entitlement of those with a shorter attachment to the labour force will normally be curtailed, adequate income protection will continue through benefits for those with a longer attachment to the labour force, and for those who reside in a region with a high rate of unemployment.
But the best way to fight unemployment is to prevent it. The federal government right now is investing well over half a billion dollars in the training and retraining of Canadians to increase their employability and income. Most of this very productive training is carried out in provincial institutions. I must say that very seldom does the federal government get any credit for this.
In the past five years government funding of industrial training has increased 500 per cent from $10 million to over the $51 million originally planned for next year. That will be increased by $19 million to a total of $70 million in 1977-78.
These training opportunities will particularly benefit young workers, women returning to new careers in the labour force, native people, and the many Canadians who each year find that they must acquire a new occupation to earn their living.
Employment and Immigration
No comprehensive employment strategy for Canada would be complete without providing more opportunities for Canadians who are, in one way or another, seriously disadvantaged in finding and keeping jobs. The Outreach Program, intensive counselling programs, the Local Employment Assistance Program, and the development community employment strategy-these are the programs that we can and should improve in order to do more for the Canadians who are hardest hit by unemployment, regardless of the state of the economy.
As these innovative measures develop and prove successful, we shall expand them as rapidly as possible. In this way we will enable yet more unemployed people to take advantage of skill development programs and job creation. The result will be a much more productive and more fully employed labour force.
Canadians are vigorous and active-although I think this is sometimes not shown on the other side of the House. They want to work, and they often need training. They deserve a decent chance to have both. The role of an employment strategy is to see that they have the fullest possible access to job opportunities. And the role of the government is to see that this strategy is developed and put into place.
In order for an over-all employment strategy to be effective, it must be administered by an efficient organization and backed by sound legislation. I urge members to support this measure as a solid contribution toward the achievement of both these aims. I am sure this government can do it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow the hon. member on the government side who just read through his speech. To save time I thought he might have appended it to the proceedings of the day. It is good to see him participate in the debate, however.
I should like to concentrate on two matters, first, the reorganization of the department as it affects immigration procedures, which is my special interest; second, unemployment insurance, both as to local organization and the eight to 12 weeks extension for attachment to the job market.
We received an organizational chart of the proposed Canada employment and immigration commission from the deputy minister, dated January 20, 1977. The first impression is of a well defined department. The flow charts are all in place. But when you analyse it further you find that the problems raised so often at the special joint committee on immigration, and the bureaucratic nightmares, will be duplicated.
The names of the deputy minister and assistant deputy minister appear in little boxes at the top of the organizational chart. But then one finds another bureaucratic layer of people with the title of executive director-there is an executive director for immigration and demographic policy with special responsibilities relating to the Immigration Act, the selection of immigrants, the resettlement of immigrants and Canada's demographic policy. Yesterday I asked the minister if we would have a demographic policy before the House at second

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
reading of Bill C-24. The minister indicated we would-if it is possible. I should like to urge the minister to have the policy and the regulations before the House at that time.
The next executive director has the title executive director of labour market policy. I understand he will look after training programs, development, counselling, placement services, employment development programs and so on. That seem to parallel closely the program that exists within the department already. And not only will we have an executive director of labour market policy but he will have an assistant executive director in charge of training programs.
There is an executive director of benefit programs primarily relating to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The small print shows that this person will be responsible for immigrant adjustment assessment or resettlement programs. One of the major criticisms heard by the committee as it met with Canadians was that the resettlement programs break down after immigrants arrive in this country. The argument was made that the best resettlement programs were those run by local community organizations interested in immigrants. This seemed to make more sense than having large bureaucratic programs put into place and operated by the department.
Then there are executive directors of national systems and services, of personnel, of finance and administrative services; as well there is an executive director general in each province and one in charge of foreign operations.
When you look at the department the minister has envisaged, not only is it going to be top heavy but, more important, it is going to be a maze, especially for immigrants. They will simply be amalgamated into programs that have high manpower orientation. I am not convinced that the high priority of manpower objectives, good though they may be, is in the best interests of immigrants. None of us quibble with the idea that in order for immigrants to be successfully resettled in Canada and have opportunities using their full potential and earning power, they must have jobs. It makes no sense for these people to be allowed to come to Canada and then to join unemployment rolls. That is not the argument. The argument is that in the manpower side of the department, the manpower mentality will become so dominant in immigrant selection that I fear the minister might be creating something with which he himself in the future will have difficulty in coping.
There are various suggestions as to reorganization, and I want to place a few on the record today, if I may. As I have indicated, I am not saying that all those executive directors are needed. I simply want to say, let us not have an over-emphasis on manpower when looking at immigrants and their needs. The special joint committee on immigration looked at the reorganization of the department and made recommendations to the minister of that day regarding this. This is clearly spelled out in the report of the special joint committee to parliament which is included in the minutes of that committee. The committee recognized that the former minister of man-
[Mr. Epp.J
power and immigration had an unduly heavy burden with regard to the myriads of programs that had attached themselves to that department, not only in the area of manpower but also with regard to unemployment insurance, which then was a separate commission but reported to the minister and which will now be amalgamated, as well as immigration, resettlement and training programs.
So no matter who the minister is, the heavy burden was recognized by the committee and recommendations were made. It was a large portfolio and a number of committee members felt that immigration linked with manpower led to an exaggerated importance being attached to employment considerations. Much of the discussion centred around this thought. For instance, Dr. Andre Raynauld, chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, had similar views when we spoke to him about it, and so did Dr. Harvey Lithwick who was at that time attached to the Toronto Board of Education. All of them seemed to indicate that while employment had to be related to the immigration selection procedure, it should not be the dominant factor.
The special joint committee said the following about departmental reorganization. This recommendation had the majority support at that time. I am quoting from the minutes of the special joint committee which met on Thursday, November 6, 1975, issue 53, page 43. It reads:
Of the several proposals put to the committee, the one which attracted most support was that immigration be detached from manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission and instead be linked with citizenship, multicultur-alism and population to form a new portfolio.
It was felt this represented a rational grouping of federal responsibilities, and a minister with such a portfolio could expect to carry considerable weight in the cabinet. Also, there was a widespread feeling that serious efforts should be made to strengthen the settlement services within the immigration branch.
Having placed the caveat that of course manpower and employment factors have to be part of the selection process, I personally favour a linking of immigration with citizenship, multiculturalism and the demographic policy. That demographic policy not only will affect the future of Canada with regard to the numbers and distribution of the population and regional requirements, but will also include the large question in Canada today of land use, and the use of both renewable and non-renewable resources. I believe that this area is one to which, I submit, we have not given sufficient thought as Canadians because we have always projected Canada to be a large country with unlimited resources but with a limited population. The point of the matter is that if we do not start making some serious studies on the question of land use as well as on the distribution of population, and how our economic policies have contributed to the movement of people to places like Toronto and the Golden Horseshoe, it is encumbent on a department of the government to look upon these human resources and twin them with Canada's natural resources. I believe it is simply too large a task to ask of one department. I favour the approach that a separate department of immigration and citizenship be formed in charge of multiculturalism and the question of the demographic policy, including land use and resource use.
February 2, 1977

There is another reason that one could give for that proposal, and that is the question of citizenship. I am sure each member of the House has been told by people who live in his or her riding, who have landed immigrant status, that when they get to the point of applying for citizenship they generally think of citizenship as a natural extension of the immigration experience. They have made contacts in the immigration department and suddenly they find that they must go to another department, in this case the Department of the Secretary of State. I think it makes more practical sense for immigration and citizenship to be a natural continuum of the experience of a person becoming an immigrant and finally a Canadian citizen. I fear that with this division between the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Department of the Secretary of State a dichotomy exists and confusion results. I think that would be another reason why that union should take place.
Another point in favour of this approach is multiculturalism. Frankly, this concept has been the whipping boy. It has been used for political purposes by the government during elections. Surely multiculturalism, and the desire to retain one's culture which is experienced in new immigrant communities, would be better served by the Department of the Secretary of State if this were part of the immigration experience, than it is today by the Department of Labour. I see no association between multiculturalism and labour. Why is it not part of the Department of Finance or of any other department? I want to stress to the minister that I believe that the reorganization of the department has not been done in the right way. As I say, a very fine academic organizational chart has been created, but is it going to serve Canadians? That is the question to which we must address ourselves. I will speak at greater length on the question of a population study when Bill C-24 is before us.
One other aspect of the reorganization of the department is the concept of the one stop service for those applying not only for unemployment insurance benefits but also for those who want to register with the Canada Manpower Centres for job acquisition and corporate job changes. I think it is important that we look at the present procedure, and I can only relate my own experiences.
Experiences might vary slightly from region to region, but in my area it goes something like this: as members of parliament we come into contact with unemployed persons, those who are applying for unemployment insurance, only when they are in trouble. We do not hear much from them until their benefits are withdrawn by the Unemployment Insurance Commission or unless they are not awarded in the first place.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: That is not the maritime experience.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I said I was talking about my experience. You can speak for yours. You have a seat here.
These people call their member of parliament, they come to his constituency office, and they ask for help. I think most members of parliament now have an arrangement with provin-
Employment and Immigration
cial offices whereby they call specific people in those unemployment insurance offices in order to dispatch as quickly as possible the claim which has been presented to them.
I can say very frankly that the person the minister has in the Winnipeg office who helps members of parliament with these problems has gone far beyond the call of duty. She has worked overtime and been very prompt, and I think she is to be commended. However, reorganization has already started and is taking place in local areas. In my area, for example, it is taking place.
What happens now is that when people are in difficulties they go to the area Canada Manpower Office wondering what to do with their problems. We have seen what has happened in those offices. They get a Winnipeg telephone number. Many of these people are already sick and tired of bureaucratic red tape. They are in a maze, they want to get out of it, but this puts them in even further. These people are unemployed; they are given a Winnipeg telephone number; but are they told to call collect? No. They are expected to spend their own money to phone Winnipeg, without any assurance that they will contact the right person or that their files will be examined quickly. Where can they go? They come back to the constituency office of their member of parliament, but they are a little more frustrated than they were before.
If the minister wants to reorganize at the local level, that is fine, but he should put insurance officers in local offices who can make decisions as to eligibility. Those officers should have the authority to say to applicants when their claims will be valid, what the weekly benefits will be, and when they can expect their money. If that does not happen and if applicants have to go back to Winnipeg, the only thing which will have been established is another layer of bureaucracy. It is vitally important that not only do we have Canada Manpower people in place but also that unemployment officers are in place locally, and that those officers can make decisions so that claims can be handled very quickly.
All of us know that unemployment creates hardship for people, and nothing is more frustrating to claimants who make applications than not knowing what is happening with their claims. If the reorganization at the local level contributes in any way to giving these people the information they deserve and to which they have a right, and if decisions as to their eligibility for benefits or as to the amount of benefits can be made quickly, the reorganization will have been worth while.
There has already been some rhetoric with regard to the change from eight weeks to twelve weeks, and I expect there will be more. One thing which is borne out very quickly is that it is much easier to put something in place than to take it away. It should be the duty of all of us, before we legislate and put a program into place, to see that that program does not create a dependency, and to see that, when that program is removed, hardship is not the result. I think there is some awareness developing that government programs which initially look advantageous, in the long term very frequently are self-defeating.

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
I want to say at the outset that I welcome and favour the change from eight weeks to 12 weeks attachment to the labour market. I support that amendment. Why? The unemployment insurance claimants who come to my office-and somebody might say that it is easy for me to talk because there is relatively little unemployment in the area I represent-fall into three general categories.
The first category comprises people who have been attached to the labour market for some period of time, in some cases years and years. Those people have made a considerable contribution to the unemployment insurance fund. They generally look upon unemployment insurance as insurance against a period of time when they are between jobs or, if there is a downturn in the economy, when they are laid off. However, in their minds it is insurance, they have paid for that insurance policy, bargained with their employers, and their employers also have contributed to that insurance policy. These people who have had a long attachment to the employment market are some of the severest critics of the present Unemployment Insurance Act because they see the insurance policy they have been buying seriously jeopardized by those who have not had the same attachment to the labour market as they have. There is no question but that I want to protect those people and the insurance that they have rightfully earned.
The second group comprises those who are chronically unemployed due to lack of training or skills, but are we providing these people with any service by marginally attaching them to the labour force so that they can collect unemployment insurance and then, once that unemployment insurance has expired, attaching them marginally once again so that the cycle continues? Is that a service? I say no. The people to whom I am now referring have a right to be trained and to develop their skills. It is a worth-while social goal to develop fully our human resources. However, is the Unemployment Insurance Act the best vehicle by which to meet that goal? I say no. I believe that the minister is correct in attempting to categorize those people who have been chronically unemployed and to give them training which will increase their attachment to the labour force, rather than simply to attach them to the labour force for brief periods which qualify them for another round of benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Then there is a third group, and I find it interesting that members of parliament can speak against the abuses of unemployment insurance so frequently when they are in their ridings. I suppose all members have had constituents coming to their offices and complaining about the abuses of unemployment insurance. I do not say that all the unemployed abuse unemployment insurance, but some do. Some try to claim unemployment insurance after a minimum attachment to the labour force. Actually, they look on unemployment insurance benefits as added income to be derived after a minimal attachment to the labour force.
People have come into my riding office asking how many weeks they must work to qualify for unemployment insurance.

I am sure most other hon. members have had similar experiences. I say openly to NDP members from Manitoba that the Manitoba government introduced a program for giving people eight weeks of work in order to remove them from welfare rolls. Yes, that has happened in Manitoba. I say that that is an abuse of unemployment insurance, and people who do that are jeopardizing those who have bought insurance. I do not think the unemployment insurance fund should be used in that manner. Let me recite another example.
Once a person came to my office with a separation slip, signed by some official working for a department of the Manitoba government, indicating that the holder of the slip had worked for eight weeks. The period of employment was shown on the slip. Looking at the calendar, it became obvious to me that the person had worked less than eight weeks; it was about seven weeks. When I informed that gentleman that he could not qualify for unemployment insurance, he said, "If that is the case I shall ask my social worker to give me another week's work, and if he does not do that, I will be back on welfare."
In the past the minimal requirement for attachment to the labour force has been a disincentive to work. I commend the minister for bringing in the 12-week qualifying period of employment. Many of our social benefit programs which help the less fortunate are excellent. On the other hand, a certain percentage of our population looks on governments or government agencies as a means of getting something for nothing. Some who have been marginally employed have looked on the unemployment insurance fund as a source of income, as a method whereby they could continue earning money after only a minimal attachment to the labour force.
Let us consider the initial benefit phase, as proposed in this bill. The new bill would change the five phases of the present program to three phases. Under the initial benefit phase provisions a person could get up to 25 weeks of benefits. Some say, "What, will they get benefits for only 25 weeks!" Mr. Speaker, 25 weeks is six months. People in my region have come into my office, wanting to hire people to fill jobs because jobs were not being filled. That has happened in my region; I do not say that is the case in all regions, but in my region it is.
Let me tell hon. members of another experiment taking place in Manitoba, involving the Manitoba government and the Department of National Health and Welfare. The experiment concerns a program known as Mini-Income. The MiniIncome program is being tried out in Dauphin, Manitoba, both in the town itself and its environs. They are finding in Dauphin, Manitoba, that a certain percentage of people who were previously employed are willing to go on mini-income. It is debatable if the program is truly serving those it was supposed to serve. Are we improving their position by putting them on the welfare rolls? The experiment is costing Canadian taxpayers $17 million. If you try to get facts concerning the program from the mini-income people, you will find that those facts are not forthcoming. All local indications show that a minimum benefit has been derived from the spending of that $17 million.
February 2, 1977

The NDP, especially, does not like the change in the minimum working requirement to 12 weeks, from eight weeks. The hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) suggested that for bringing in this provision the government ought to be tried under a section of the Criminal Code. But the hon. member's party thinks that only one agency, government, can create jobs. Mr. Speaker, such reliance on government must be reduced. With all due respect, we already have in this country the LIP program, Canada Works, Young Canada Works, FLIP, LEAP and many other programs. The question is, are we helping Canadians to obtain long-term jobs?
Without doubt, benefits were flowing from the operations of citizen advisory group committees when local projects were undertaken. After all, it is better to have people working than to have them on unemployment insurance. But the essential point remains to be considered, and it is this: we must find a new climate in this country, Mr. Speaker, and that new climate can only be created by the private sector. I know that we shall see joint ventures involving governments at all levels and the private sector. The point is that all relevant figures show that private investment is down.
We know that investment has declined. People are holding back, not investing. Mr. Speaker, nothing reduces available jobs and creates a downturn in the economy more quickly than a loss of investor confidence. The minister can bring forward all sorts of make-work programs which will give temporary relief, it is true, but they are not the long-term solution for which we are looking.
We hear a lot these days about people being ripped off. The one being ripped off is the worker, the person who goes to his job day after day. When jobs are placed in jeopardy because of a lack of investment, it is the worker who suffers first. There is no question about it.
We must return to where employment is created in the private sector. This will mean a reduction in the demands of all governments at all levels on the production of all Canadians. We are now at a level where all levels of government demand 42 per cent of the gross national product. I say to the government, freeze it!
The fact that the economy would grow would not only increase revenues for governments at all levels, but would allow each individual and each corporation to start making more of its own decisions. They cannot make those decisions if 42 per cent is taken off the top. It is the other 58 per cent that they need simply to stay alive. However, that does not build confidence in investments.
The minister spoke at some length about a new employment strategy, the work-sharing experiments for example. To my way of thinking, work-sharing indicates partial defeat. It also indicates that large pools of labour will be asked to reduce their productivity. Rather, the reverse action should be taken.
