speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will just be another minute or two.
Let us improve the productivity of workers and create investment confidence. A number of representations have been made to the minister regarding exactly this point. In most cases they have said that unemployment insurance as presently constituted has not only become a very costly way of doing business but has reduced investment confidence.
Our unemployment rate goes up possibly most dramatically when construction in Canada is faltering. There is no greater indicator of unemployment difficulties than when construction is faltering. The Canadian Construction Association stated very clearly that they are in favour of the increase from eight to 12 weeks and the development of confidence of which I have spoken. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business, a large organization of small business interests in Canada creating many thousands of jobs, are in favour of the eight to 12 week amendment. I could go on. There is the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. These are all private industries.
What about the Canadian Labour Congress? The Canadian Labour Congress also analysed it. The person to which they have first responsibility is the one who paid his dues for years and years to that congress. That person today is seriously questioning why he has to work day in and day out. Others who worked with him were able to leave the labour market and literally thumb their noses at him saying, "Why work? It is just as good on unemployment insurance". Let us bring back an intelligent policy for those who have earned it. I hope these amendments will go a long way in that direction.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the main points of this bill concern, first, the reorganization of UIC and Manpower offices into an integrated setup; two, increasing the entrance requirement for receiving UIC benefits from eight to 12 weeks; three, reducing the number of benefit weeks payable while simplifying the benefit structure; and, four, providing for the payment of UIC benefits to those on training, in work-sharing agreements and in job training projects.
The first thing I want to say about this act is that it, in itself, is a prime example of how the economic and social policies of the Liberal government under the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had been marked by inconsistency, flip flops and excessive ad hocery. The following are some examples.
One, wage and price controls were considered as no good for the country, and then they were implemented.
Two, in 1973 we were told that there were plenty of Canadian oil reserves well into the future, but by 1975 we had become a net importer of oil.
Three, tax laws were reformed with the closing of loopholes for the rich, and then the effects of these reforms were thrown

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
out the window when recent budgets introduced new ones like RHOSP and RRSP, and taking the 10 per cent surtax off those who make more than $30,000 in Bill C-22.
Four, job creation programs, both for adults and students, were established, then cut back and abolished, and then restored again.
Five, in this bill the government is combining the UIC operations and manpower. It is doing another flip flop and admitting a costly mistake was made in separating them in 1966. Of course the public has to pay for the reintegration of these offices.
Six, unemployment insurance was substantially broadened in 1971, then significantly narrowed again last year, and made even more narrow in the bill that is before us today.
My major concern about this bill is not with the reorganization mentioned earlier, or even with the question of paying UIC benefits to those on training, in work-sharing agreements and job creation projects. My hon. colleague, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), dealt with those in leading off the debate for our party yesterday. I want, instead, to put emphasis on the changing entrance requirements from eight to 12 weeks, and the reduction of the number of benefit weeks payable under the new streamlined benefit structure. Later, if I have time I may comment on some of the former.
Any MP from the Atlantic region, except perhaps those representing the few metropolitan areas in those provinces, knows that such changes can be a grave threat to seasonal workers in that region. This generalization will also hold for areas in Quebec and possibly others such as northern Ontario, and possibly remote northern areas of some of the western provinces.
When the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) first introduced notice of the changes on Thursday, December 9, the minister of labour for the province of Nova Scotia was quoted as saying on the front page of the Halifax Herald that such a move at this time could impose serious economic hardships in Nova Scotia, and I quote:
The timing is wrong, many people who want jobs can't get them-the real unemployment figures are soaring ... it's not just people who don't want to work.
Mr. Fitzgerald also said, and I quote:
The provincial social services department will have to pick up the slack for many jobless people left without UIC payments under the proposed changes.
I suggest that if the Liberal minister of labour for the province of Nova Scotia is right, then we can expect even more severe problems in New Brunswick, and, especially in the northern areas represented by Liberal members. Last week end I was in the Chatham-Newcastle area and the unemployment in these northshore Miramichi communities is up to a sickening 30 to 35 per cent.
Recently a team of New Democratic Party members of parliament were looking at the situation in Newfoundland. The increased entrance requirement to 12 weeks from eight

weeks will adversely affect many Newfoundland communities dependent upon fishing and fish processing. Outport communities such as St. Anthony and Twillingate, and indeed the whole north and northeast coast of Newfoundland, will be hit by nothing short of a disaster if these amendments are passed. In past years this coastline has sometimes been icebound till June, enabling fish plants to work only ten weeks, or less. This situation will certainly arise again in the future and the fish plant workers, through no fault of their own, will not be able to qualify for UIC benefits to see them through the long hard winter.
How Liberal or Conservative members of parliament from Newfoundland could support this piece of legislation, which will hit their province harder than any other in Canada, is beyond my comprehension. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) must be very familiar with this problem. In his constituency of Burin-Burgeo there is a fish plant at Isle aux Morts in which the workers are lucky to get eight to ten weeks employment because the federal government has allowed the herring stock to become so depleted. What will the hon. gentleman tell these workers when they will not be eligible for unemployment next year? It truly will be an Isle aux Morts in any language.
One of the sweeteners in this bill, which, in general, is a sour one, is that there will be a saving through reduction in the employer-employee premiums. For example, it would be $4 million in Newfoundland and $7.7 million in Nova Scotia. But each of these provinces in turn would see a reduction in unemployment insurance payouts resulting from the new amendment which would amount to between $24 million and $28 million in Newfoundland and between $9 million and $11 million in Nova Scotia. Manpower Department figures for the first five months of 1976 showed that 63.8 per cent of all eight to 11 weekers were in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces- areas with extremely low job vacancy levels and endemic histories of seasonal unemployment.
Taking the employer-employee reductions in the Atlantic region and Quebec, we find that $85,800,000 will be saved through reduced premiums but that $175 million is taken away from those provinces by these amendments. This means that taking only the effects of this bill into account there will be $89,500,000 less multiplying around in these provincial economies because of these changes.
These total figures for the Atlantic provinces and Quebec are the result not only of the changes in the qualification period but are also attributable to the reduction of benefits envisaged in this bill. No one would argue against simplifying the benefit structure for unemployment insurance payments. However, in simplifying the benefit structure by eliminating the national extended benefit period, the government has also reduced benefits for more recipients.
The minister and his departmental employees have tried to argue that tying special extended benefits to regional unemployment rates rather than the national rate would automatically result in longer benefit periods in areas of high unemployment such as the Atlantic provinces and part of Quebec.
February 2, 1977

As far as I am concerned, they are playing with words. It is true there would be shorter benefit periods in areas of relatively low unemployment such as the prairies, but this would be offset by the fact that the high unemployment areas in the Atlantic region would be still tied to a definition of a region which makes the region equivalent to the province.
For example, the Statistics Canada labour force survey in the province of Nova Scotia divides the area geographically into four groups, plus the Halifax-Dartmouth area. The provincial unemployment average is lower than the actual unemployment in many regions of the province. This is because of the traditionally low unemployment in the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area. In effect, ridings of high unemployment such as Cape Breton-East Richmond, Cape Breton-Highlands-Canso and Cape Breton-The Sydneys do not get their true share of funds through the regional rate of unemployment criterion. For example, in 1976 the average unemployment for the province of Nova Scotia was 9.6 per cent. However, it was 12.7 per cent in Cape Breton Island as compared with only 7.2 per cent for the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area. These, of course, are official statistics and I do not wish to belabour the point that they surely do not reveal the true unemployment picture there. My point is reasonable and important for all UIC recipients there.
Since the bill does not change the definition of the region and follow the labour force survey method of determining sub-regional unemployment, the UIC recipient receives less because, to repeat, the relatively low unemployment area of the Halifax-Dartmouth metropolitan area consistently pulls down the average of unemployment in the province. Since part of the UIC payment is based on these averages, rather than on the statistics taken by the labour force survey for the whole of Cape Breton, people down there suffer. They suffer in two ways. They don't have the jobs and they don't get the amount of unemployment insurance that should be due to them. As a consequence, unemployment insurance fails to play the role of a local stabilizer in the economy that it should.
I cannot understand why the minister does not base the regional benefit on the labour force survey areas, which give a truer picture of the sub-regional unemployment within provinces. Given the fact that the Statistics Canada labour force survey is to be extended, by March, to cover some 55,000 homes instead of 40,000, this is an ideal time to make the UIC payout in these hard hit areas more realistically and fiscally responsible.
Even given this failure, there is no way the minister and his top officials should leave the impression with the public that the changing of the benefit structure is an improvement for areas like the Atlantic region.
The facts are simply these, and no amount of bureaucratic gobbledygook from high paid civil servants is going to change it. Under the present scheme, and I am referring now to the one which is currently operating, a person in Cape Breton who has worked for 20 weeks would get 51 weeks benefit. Under the bill before us, on the other hand, Bill C-27, the person who worked 20 weeks would only be entitled to 38-40 weeks.
Employment and Immigration
Similarly the person who worked for 12 weeks under the present scheme would get 44 weeks of benefit while under Bill C-27 the person who worked for 12 weeks would be entitled to only 30-32 weeks of benefit.
As if that were not bad enough, Mr. Speaker, I must express my anger at the present minister who, on a one-to-one basis, is generally more personable than most Liberal cabinet ministers. I am angry with him because he keeps trying to defend these changes by referring to the fact that only "kids and housewives" will be affected by this reduction in benefits. Not only is the minister's statement inaccurate but it smacks of discrimination. A young man who is 17 or 18 years of age is not considered a kid by the government if he has to fight for his country. Housewives who are among the far greater number of women in the labour force, especially in areas of high unemployment like the Atlantic provinces, work to supplement the family income. It is more than chauvinistic; it is very wrong for the minister's advisers to assume that these housewives would not want to work in order to supplement the family income at a time of high living costs, high educational costs for their children, and the high cost of everything in our economy today.
It is all right for an MP or top level civil servant whose wife does not have to join the labour force, and whose family income is naturally high because the chief breadwinner's income is high, to use the criteria or yardstick of the income of the breadwinner to determine the economic welfare of the family. But I want to tell the minister and his associates in the strongest possible terms, and with the deepest conviction, that they are wrong. They are using a double standard of economic welfare that discriminates against these housewives who want to work and these kids, so-called, between the ages of 17 and 22.
Recently on our visit to Newfoundland we had a well presented brief from a pro-femina group who were attached to the manpower department in St. John's. They told us without equivocation that the surveys that they have made among housewives in the Newfoundland area indicate that over 50 per cent of the housewives surveyed would like either to enter or re-enter the labour force. As the hon. member for Nickel Belt mentioned yesterday, Statistics Canada published a study of unemployment this past August comparing 1973 with 1971, and one of their conclusions was that in both years unemployed wives tended to come from families with low incomes.
The discrimination against young adults and housewives which is in this bill seems to be added to by the inaccuracy of the minister's statement about the composition of those who are to be desentitled. In June, 1976, a month when many students were on the job market and unemployed in large numbers, only 12.5 per cent of unemployment insurance recipients were under 20 years of age. Adult males made up 45.8 per cent of the total recipients, and adult women accounted for 41.7 per cent.

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
When these changes are viewed from a regional and subregional perspective, they become even more significant. The government tries to play all kinds of statistical games by giving a selective profile of these eight to 12 insured weeks applicants. These profiles say that 64 per cent of all these applicants in 1974 had dropped out of the labour force by March, 1975. This, I suggest, is due to the fact that the national economy is performing so badly under this government that the incidence of the discouraged worker withdrawing from the labour force is increasing. The Nova Scotia department of labour publishes monthly current labour force statistics for the province, and in November they included the following note explaining what seemed to be a decline in the unemployment rate in Cape Breton:
However, the figure for Cape Breton is very misleading if one were to look at the participation rate next to the unemployment rate. The participation rate in Cape Breton fell by 4.3 percentage points and thus, accounts for the fall in the unemployment rate. The fall in the participation rate can mean that people in Cape Breton feel that there is no need to look for work because there are no potential jobs in the area, so they fall out of the labour force. Again, one can see the effect of the economic slowdown in that many people are now falling out of the labour force as discouraged workers. A fall in the labour force of the potential unemployed (that would be counted as unemployed if they stayed in the labour force) means a fall in the unemployment rate.
The federal Department of Manpower refuses to acknowledge that the recession is forcing thousands not just on to the unemployment rolls but out of the labour force entirely. They argue that they are trying, through this method of reducing the qualification for benefits by pushing the period up to 12 weeks from eight weeks, to improve the labour force attachment of this group. Indeed, one can view this move against the eight to 12 weekers as an attempt to force them into withdrawing from the labour force faster, and thus erasing the government's embarrassment over their failure to provide Canadian jobs. This is going to affect over 330,000 Canadians in the course of a year, not 50,000, as the minister keeps repeating.
A Canadian Press report yesterday had this to say on this question:
Estimates of the number of claimants who would be cut from unemployment insurance payments as a result of the change range from 50,000 to 330,000.
So the figure could be 330,000, although the figure that the minister used at one time was 50,000. Let us not be fooled by the way the minister and his departmental advisers are using these statistics; some 330,000 are going to be affected by this measure although it would be only 50,000 at a particular time.
The Department of Manpower states that almost half these people are under the age of 25, and that many are working wives and young persons working at home as I have already said. What is left unsaid, however, is that over half are over 25, 75,000 are between the ages of 25 and 34, 41,000 between the ages of 35 and 44, 35,000 between the ages of 45 and 54, and 19,000 are between 55 and 64. As for the charge that some of these people are only a second income to the family, a kind of secondary worker, according to the 1971 census 6,200 heads of households in my riding-and I am sure this would apply to the riding of the hon. member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. MacEachen)-draw less than $5,800. Surely these families should not be denied a second source of

income by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), or the Liberal cabinet.
Further, the minister says that only 30 per cent eight to 12 weekers have established a season repeat pattern. This amounts to a total of 110,000 Canadians in the course of one year, 110,000 people who will probably not be able to remain where they are to work those eight to 12 weeks per year, if this measure passes. Has the minister given any thought to what will happen to these seasonal enterprises if the people can no longer stay in the area to work for the two months required, since, this would not provide the necessary number of stamps to carry that person over the winter?
Further, it is alleged by the department that these changes would result, at most, in an additional 2 to 3 per cent in social assistance costs. The federal government is arbitrarily shifting financial burdens to the provinces and municipalities, and then it wonders why a significant segment of Quebec views federalism as a deadend street. Such narrow-mindedness on the part of the federal government helps sow a bitter harvest. The municipalities in my own riding can scarcely afford this increase, even without an Olympic debt. Their industrial tax base is declining, and you can only levy so much property tax before it becomes self-defeating.
Canada is a large country with regional economies that are not always in step. The former minister of manpower and immigration, now the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), promised in the budget speech that the so-called four weeks rule would be abolished. This rule now means that an individual who does not receive extended benefits for four weeks, or more, has his claim permanently terminated. Experience has indicated that this rule clearly served as a deterrent for claimants to return to short-term work that lasts more than four weeks and now less than 12. This is the regulation that caused Cape Breton steelworkers to be cut off their unemployment insurance, as reported in the Cape Breton Post on August 10, 1976, after being recalled to the steel plant for a short period of employment, so we are happy about that change and the change regarding severance pay as well.
The "work-sharing scheme" of this bill-under which a private employer can draw part of his wage bill from the unemployment insurance account-is full of pitfalls and opportunities for abuse. It will probably turn out to be like some of the projects on retraining on the job, or like "experience rating"-the idea that employers with lower rates of employee turnover should pay lower premiums. This well-intentioned tinkering with local job markets has now fortunately been scrapped.
The minister, of course, will answer that the new Canada Works program, which in essence is an extended LIP project, and the Young Canada Works program, in the Atlantic region will soften some of the dire effects that could ensue from these changes. I do not blame the present minister, but it surely is the height of departmental inefficiency to have rushed the
February 2, 1977

application date of Young Canada Works as they have done. The high school and college age groups have not had sufficient time, or counselling with manpower and other groups, to come up with projects that could qualitatively improve their own skills and at the same time best help their communities.
Last week in Cape Breton I was trying to get the high schools to move on this because the cut-off date is February 4. All kinds of people were coming to me and asking what they could do. I am not blaming the new minister, for this, but there should have been some planning over the past five months so that there could be many qualitative as well as quantitative projects to improve the total community. The whole Young Canada Works program is now a complete administrative snafu.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote from a recent editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen, which usually supports the Liberal government, and which is entitled "More Band-Aids For The Jobless". It reads:
Manpower Minister Bud Cullen, like so many before him, mistakenly believes temporary job schemes solve this country's chronic unemployment problems.
New Democratic Party Leader Ed Broadbent aptly calls these programs "handouts". He suggests the government might spend its time more profitably adopting policies to ensure that Canadians can find the jobs they want.
The newest package involves allocating $350 million to such programs as Canada Works, Young Canada Works and summer job corps. A bit far-fetched from a government which only a year ago killed the Company of Young Canadians, in the name of restraint, to save $130 million.
Mr. Cullen says the new program differs from the old ones because of "a permanency we never had in the past". The only hint of permanency is a commitment to a five-year program of temporary job creation.
Ultimately, the government's attitude is the downfall of this system. The Company of Young Canadians case is the classic example: such programs are the first to go when budgets or ministerial portfolios are juggled.
The Liberals should learn from past experience the inconsistency with which funds were distributed and the inherent opportunities for patronage dictate the need for real employment to offer workers the benefits and security enjoyed by those now in the labour force.
I was not surprised but was somewhat amused by the remarks of the Conservative manpower critic in the House yesterday. As the Canadian Press report in today's Citizen puts it, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) claims that his party should get the credit for the proposal to toughen unemployment benefits because he had called for such measures since 1971.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) says he agrees with the provision of eight to 12 weeks; what he did not say in the House but did say to the press was that he wanted 20 weeks. He says this has little to do with the fact that he comes from an area which enjoys relatively high employment. I wonder if members of that party from Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces would say that.
The bill before us is essentially another example of the inconsistency, of the flip flops and excessive ad hoc arrangement and band-aid applications used by the government as substitutes for policies of full employment and economic stability for the Canadian people. Whatever the virtues, political or otherwise, that the Prime Minister is considered to have by his cabinet and backbenchers, and by his followers, principally
Employment and Immigration
in Quebec, he certainly has made a mess of managing economic policy in this country. When he came to office we had the second highest standard of living in the developed world-as measured by per person income; today we are in the eighth place.
The latest available United Nations bulletin of statistics is for 1975. It shows that there were 13 nations in the world with lower unemployment rates than Canada.
Last year the Economic Council of Canada issued a paper entitled "People and Jobs-A Study of the Canadian Labour Market". At page 39 it had this to say, and the Minister of Manpower chose to ignore the advice:
It would, of course, be possible to try to eliminate abuses by cutting certain categories of claimants, or the duration of benefits, or by extending the period of* work before claimants become eligible for benefits. But such recommendations could prove harmful to persons most exposed to period and genuinely involuntary employment. It would seem better to go after malingerers more directly. For this reason we believe that much of the problem of abuse of unemployment insurance could be solved by two methods-by tightening of administration efforts to get persons back to work and by creating jobs to absorb them.
To that I say amen, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I read carefully the best speech my colleague from Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) ever made. I found it so thorough that I shall not go over the topics he dealt with. He denounced the ambiguity of the Unemployment Insurance Act and fustigated the regulations written by the technocrats for being three times as voluminous as the act itself. And to think that all that was done in an attempt to avoid paying the unemployed the benefits they are entitled to. The member for Kamouraska is a former union president, in addition to which he sat on the board of arbitration for several years. In other words, Mr. Speaker, he knows what he is talking about. I shall therefore limit my remarks this afternoon to the object of the bill, unemployment insurance with regard to work.
The minister entitles his bill:
An Act to establish the Department of Employment.. .
The minister thinks he is changing the spirit of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I say the expression "Department of Employment" is even less true than "unemployment insurance" because at least unemployment really exists while employment is nonexistent most of the time. A while ago I heard the former speaker preaching full employment. I always find that slightly amusing under present circumstances. Why think, consider or even believe in full employment? Everything modern should then be completely eliminated. A stop should be put to the invasion of the labour market by the machine which does away completely with some workers; all scientific processes should be done away with if we want to have full employment and go back 50 or 75 years to the days when, for instance, sand was still carried about in little round shovels: that is humanly and economically impossible. So why talk and try to argue in favour of full employment? It is pointless.

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Everybody knows very well for that matter that unemployment, just as welfare, which is its corollary, is the result of our era of automation which creates affluence and leisure. The present state of unemployment therefore demonstrates without doubt that we are fifty years late in adapting our economy to our social reforms and our social reforms to the scientific development we have known for the last fifty years. All this is due to our inability or reluctance to free ourselves from the old principles of the society based on production for the sake of profit that we have known. We are then forced to think out such ridiculous and temporary devices as unemployment insurance, which has the effect of a palliative in a nonevolving society.
Above all, let us not try to have people believe that the government will replace unemployment by full employment. Within the framework of our society where production is aimed at profit, it is impossible to talk about full employment. Let us then talk about full income or a minimum guaranteed income for all, but not about full employment for all.
In spite of all the efforts made by capitalist governments which have always sacrificed human capital to money capital, these gentlemen will be forced by events and by universal logic to agree with social credit proposals, namely the establishment of a dividend for everyone. This dividend will have to be distributed according to the income of Canada rather than be based on set premiums like present unemployment insurance. In fact, when unemployment insurance ceases, that is to say when the claimant can no longer receive benefits, he must necessarily begin to live on welfare. In other words he begins to receive a small national dividend. What people on welfare receive is a small national dividend which comes from the national product and which is the precursor of a dividend for everyone.
I am saying that unemployment insurance is a band-aid treatment because either the real cure has not been discovered or, which is worse, we did not want to apply the real and only cure possible because of stronger financial motivation. I say that these governments behave like criminals towards society.
Perhaps they will tell us that they ignored these data which would have enabled our society to move at the same pace as our scientific emancipation in all aspects of electronics and automation. However it was foreseeable that the more the machine would replace human energy, the smaller the number of workers who would have to sacrifice their lives to feed the rest of mankind. Today, I am well aware that several people in governments would have benefited from learning by heart the works of Major C. H. Douglas because they would have understood fifty years ago what they begin to grasp today.
People have always imagined that the founder of social credit was concerned only about the monetary system, which is untrue since this matter takes up only ten pages in his treatise. He talked mostly about economic and fiscal reforms, about social reforms to follow scientific innovation and to live with

automation which was beginning at that time, and we can conclude from this that the national dividend is the only solution to all job losses caused by automation.
He even talked about unemployment and leisure. This is why I was pleasantly surprised when the minister, in introducing his new Bill C-27, told us about the three programs which he wanted to emphasize, that is recycling or adult training, the leisure fund and job sharing. I therefore congratulate the minister and urge him to continue in this direction. Indeed I would very much like to know if he has read the chapter on leisure and intellectual liberation in the book by Mr. Douglas. In this chapter, we see that it is not an exaggeration to say that 75 per cent of the new ideas, and even the inventions to which humanity owes its progress, can be attributed to unemployed people. As a matter of fact, this is what has enabled us to leave the age of the muscle which benefited a few people and to enter the age of automation, where science should serve everyone. Suggesting that we should keep an outdated and obsolete organization system because of the risk involved is like refusing to build a railway because of the unfavourable effects on stage-coach transportation. I have every confidence that the minister, who is young and full of vigour, will continue to open up new avenues and to find inspiration in the book by C. H. Douglas. If he does not have it, I can give it to him. This book was written 50 years ago, but it is now even more relevant than ever.
In the meantime, I understand that we have to operate as well as we can with the old tools designed by the financial controllers who lead the governments according to their will and the vagaries of their capital. For them, man has always been a simple production tool to enable them to increase their capital, but in the new society created by automation, man will give much more importance to intelligence and sports. I think the minister has just become aware of this, because once they are free from their total involvement in the work which gave them shelter, clothing, food and basic necessities, tomorrow's men and women will be able to spend more time on creative endeavours.
It is up to the government to further direct its efforts towards social security for all citizens rather than acting as a protector of money capital. I would like to add a few words about new programs such as Canada Works and Young-Canada Works. I think these programs are transitory but necessary incentives which will benefit the population provided they are well administered. They will reduce unemployment, using the same money but at least the unemployed will be given a chance to keep busy while producing useful goods. Still I am quite anxious to see what direction will be given to these projects. As I see it, the people of the area concerned are in the best position to advise the minister on that.
I think that Canada Works should be meshed with the other program over the summer months to make it possible to direct the efforts of both groups towards a sole objective. It would be unfortunate for instance if student projects could not be meshed with or even, depending on circumstances, incorporated into those of Canada Works. Therefore we urge the
February 2, 1977

minister to encourage students to work in their respective municipality even if their activities do not coincide with their field of studies. I think 1 heard that student projects cannot be consistent with other endeavours under Canada Works because students must work within their field of interest so that it be a follow-up of their studies. Mr. Speaker, I do not see why a medical student for instance could not plant trees, work on green spaces or do whatever may be worthwhile for his town or his community.
Mr. Speaker, I think that having groups of students work within their municipalities will make them proud to see that they have built something; for when they become adults they will come back in their communities and say: we did that for our own community. And I think it is fine for students, even if they do not make direct use of the knowledge they may have acquired during the school year. I am sure the minister will consider these remarks. I think he agrees with all of us that these projects should not be launched simply to provide employment but rather to leave something in their communities.
We need these projects very badly. I know some in my region which two or three departments may be interested in, be it forestry, environment or green spaces; I know there are many thorough projects that will undoubtedly interest the department, but to do that, both groups must not be opponents or competitors. The projects should be easily merged so that we can do serious work at the municipal level. I am prepared to believe that regional officers do their best to satisfy recipients, although there are some-and thank goodness they are the exception to the rule!-who tell our voters that the MP has no right to interfere in such matter. When it comes to projects like the one pertaining to unemployment insurance, I do believe-and so does the minister since he uses our services so often and I commend him for it-that a certain propaganda goes on at the regional level and I know very well from the start that the minister takes absolutely no notice of it. In any case, as I said earlier, we simply must do something about unemployment insurance.
All these officials do their best, it is quite evident, and I am even prepared to give the benefit of the doubt and excuse the ignorance of those who would not let the MP look into their affairs, but they should try to understand that having voted a certain law the MP must first of all see that the law is enforced fairly and then check to see if it would not be necessary to amend it to make it clearer for the officials concerned and more flexible for the recipient.
That is a role as I see it, although some may choose not to assume it, saying that there are enough civil servants around to do the job; the choice is theirs. But I cannot shirk my duties. In any case, I can speak freely on this subject since I am generally satisfied with the work of the majority of officials in my region. I also wish to tell the minister that we are satisfied with the withdrawal of the regulation concerning the four week period of employment. We have asked for a long time
Employment and Immigration
that this regulation be abolished, since it caused so many injustices for certain recipients.
Finally, with regards to the right of appeal, we are glad to see that we will finally be able to appeal to the Federal Court even if the ruling of the board of referees is unanimous. What nonsense when, after having argued a case before the board of referees and even when the board was unanimous, it was absolutely necessary to get the permission of the chairman of the board-who had just concurred with the board-in order to go before another court! The minister now proposes to amend the regulation. Well, we discussed this during our last party caucus and did consider introducing a motion to that effect in the House. That is why I say we are fully satisfied with the change at this stage.
As for the 12 week eligibility period for benefits, it will certainly be an handicap for a great many workers in my area.
I am referring to the hundreds of people who travel to Ontario to work during the fruit and vegetable picking season. Because the season lasts only two months, or two and a half months at the most, it will be very difficult for those workers to complete the twelve week minimum period. This will affect Ontario producers as well because they will not be able to get the skilled labour they need to bring in their crops.
In addition to diverting workers to welfare, this will force the Ontario growers either to hire off-shore labour or to leave the crops in the fields. The committee should look very closely into the matter, and I would like to call the minister's attention on this. As I said, this is a most serious problem in our area. It has far reaching consequences for Ontario and raises grave concerns in our sector.
I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words on work terminations. Whether the minister gave orders or not to convince workers they should obtain the work termination form at all cost from their employers, UIC offices require that unemployed workers do everything in their power to obtain those forms. Indeed, I read the advertisements published by the government on this subject. In my view, they are misleading. Signs were put up urging workers to obtain the work termination form from their employers when they become unemployed.
Unless the act has been changed, certainly the employer must send that form to the UIC's regional office. Of course the worker should ask for it before leaving, but most of the time the employer is not ready to give it to him. In the case of a forest worker for instance he will go home, the camp will close down, and the worker will wait. Fifteen days later he will find the office does not have his work termination form, and he will be told to go back to the employer and ask for it. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the claimant should not have to do that. He has to go through it once, but, the second time, the employer has the responsibility to send a separation notice to the regional office. If he fails to do so, he should be fined. If the employer is at fault, it is the responsibility of regional officials to force employers to obey the law.

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
There have been so many abuses in this field lately that we wonder why officials seem so reluctant to fine unscrupulous employers. I have even heard of cases, which are fairly typical in my area, where they paid their workers cash instead of by cheque. In this way, the employee cannot prove that he has been working when he loses his job after eight or ten weeks. He is not eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. I asked the commission to investigate theses cases; I told them the time had come to call in the RCMP, but they never did investigate. Those guys are taking advantage of the workers as much as they like, and the poor fellows have to go on welfare, after working for eight, ten, fifteen or even as much as twenty weeks.
Yet they never miss a chance to penalize claimants, we know that, to fine them right and left. But I have never seen an employer penalized. I do not know if sometimes some of them are penalized because they are late. We should probably start by penalizing the government of Quebec, they invariably take a month and a half to send employment terminations to their employees. When you think, Mr. Speaker, that those employees cannot draw a penny as long as their employment termination slip has not reached the office although they reported immediately after leaving their job. I do hope this matter will also be considered by the standing committee so an amendment if necessary can be brought in to further protect the claimant.
I would like to say a last word on vacation pay. This is another injustice being perpetrated upon the claimant. Everyone knows that the law now allows subtracting a number of weeks proportionate to the amount of vacation pay received by the worker. I am now advising employers to pay the vacation pay every month. The vacation pay is money earned. There are four, five or six months of vacation pay. What is the loss resulting from that vacation pay? To the worker it represents a loss of one week, two weeks, three weeks or four weeks of unemployment insurance. But let him draw immediately that vacation pay so that when he is unemployed he will have no more vacation pay. This is a monumental farce. It is robbery- I call it robbery. I thought the vacation pay compensated for the two-week waiting period. But no, that vacation pay can result in a penalty of four weeks, plus a two-week waiting period, which means six weeks before getting unemployment insurance. I find that absolutely illogical. Once again, I ask the minister and the committee to consider that matter very seriously.
Finally, in concluding I want to say to the minister that we welcome the combining as well as the decision to combine both offices, namely the Canada Manpower Centre and the unemployment insurance office. That is the way it was at the beginning. It is funny how the administration works. It was like that at the beginning; in my area we only had one unemployment insurance office. After much claiming and begging, it was finally divided into two. It was supposed to be subdivided into three, but no, things have stalled. We are still waiting. But now it has been decided to re-unite the two offices. I think it is essential. They work in the same field:

unemployment and employment are in the same area. I have never known why the departments had put a partition between the two, an impassable barrier, to the point that some officers used to tell us: I cannot get the information; you should call the Manpower Centre to get such and such information. If the minister has decided to re-unite those two offices, I think a serious problem will then be settled, and the officers will provide a better service. First of all, it seems to me that a little less staff will be needed, for in my riding three or four more officers would have been needed to have an efficient UIC office, whereas with the reunification we will even save money.
Once again I want to thank the minister for having thought about it and I hope that when the committee completes its consideration we will have the amendments we want incorporated in the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose it can be said that the further one gets west, the more one's enthusiasm for this bill increases. That is understandable because the further west you get the lower the rate of unemployment becomes. Consequently, we have in effect a real dichotomy with this kind of a bill, the real regional disparities that exist in this country.
That is not to suggest we do not share the concern of other hon. members about the need to reform the Unemployment Insurance Act. There is a legitimate need for reform, a legitimate need to tighten up this legislation. I wish to quote from a study by the Economic Council of Canada in their report "People and Jobs" which came out early in 1976. It states this at page 39;
It would, of course, be possible to try to eliminate abuses by cutting certain categories of claimants or the duration of benefits, or by extending the period of work before claimants become eligible for benefits. But such recommendations could prove harmful to persons most exposed to periodic and genuinely involuntary unemployment. It would seem better to go after "malingerers" more directly. For this reason we believe that much of the problem of abuse of unemployment insurance could be solved by two methods-by tightening administrative efforts to get persons back to work, and by creating jobs to absorb them.
That says it all. I believe the need is there to tighten up the Unemployment Insurance Act. Obviously the administrative mechanism needs tightening up. It is a fact that there are abuses, but this is not the time to tamper with the provisions of this bill whereby the qualifying period for unemployment insurance is increased from eight to 12 weeks.
Obviously that is a needed reform, but that reform should not be brought in at a time of critically high unemployment, a time when this country is facing a rate of unemployment projected to be in excess of 8 per cent, a time when unemployment in my province is more than twice the national average by the present Statistics Canada yardstick of measurement.
In actual fact the real rate of unemployment in the province of Newfoundland is more like 35 per cent if you consider that we have over 55,000 people out of a work force of 183,000 drawing unemployment insurance benefits at this time.
February 2, 1977

Another 10,000 people are drawing short-term or able bodied assistance.
In the few minutes I have left to me today I would like to speak in support of and commend to the House the very reasonable and humane amendment put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander). That amendment would provide a lever whereby the minister with the approval of the governor in council and the cabinet would have the discretion of applying that particular provision of the bill, the eight week qualifying period, only to areas where unemployment was critically high. It would give the minister the discretion of having the eight week period in areas designated by him. You could use the unemployment insurance areas that presently exist as a means of measurement. In so doing, the minister would have the discretion of keeping in effect the eight week provision.
I hope that amendment will commend itself to the House. It is a reasonable compromise to those who are enthusiastic about reform and to those of us who believe it is not the time to bring in that particular reform. I hope the amendment put forward by my colleague on behalf of my party will commend itself to members of the House.
I hope it will commend itself to members opposite who come from constituencies in the Atlantic provinces where unemployment is criticially high and job prospects are dismal. I hope it will commend itself to members from the province of Quebec where the problem is equally critical. We have had projections from the C. D. Howe Institute to the effect that unemployment will increase in Quebec to 11 per cent, and in Newfoundland to a total in excess of 14 per cent on an annual basis.
I know that some members opposite feel as I do. Many of them are genuinely concerned. They have to face their constituents. They have the same problem of unemployment that I have in my constituency. If these members feel inclined to support this amendment, perhaps it may even commend itself to the minister. It may even stimulate them to break ranks with their fellows and thus ensure that the amendment will be accepted by the House.
I have talked about the unemployment rate in my province. I can only speak from experience with programs already being administered by the minister. The LIP program, for example, is presently functioning on the basis of high unemployment regions, regions which have unemployment of 7 per cent or 7.5 per cent, which happens to be the national average. These constituencies will receive additional funds. Even on the basis of that methodology, my constituency, which is a way up there, currently qualifies for almost $4 million in LIP grants. That shows the degree of recognition by the government of the unemployment situation which prevails in my province.
It is interesting to note that the last time a government bill was before the House to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act the persons hardest hit were those most severely affected by high unemployment. I refer to the amendment brought down in the fall of 1975. At that time the House was faced
Employment and Immigration
with amendments the effect of which was to remove two groups from the eligibility list, first, old age pensioners, and, second, those in that special category who had the right to receive additional unemployment insurance grants because they had five or more dependants.
The region hardest hit by the removal of those two groups from the rolls was, again, the Atlantic provinces. For example, the removal of benefits from those over 65 years of age cost the four Atlantic provinces $7,270,000, broken down as follows: Newfoundland, $1,600,000; Prince Edward Island, $600,000; Nova Scotia, $3 million, and New Brunswick, $3 million. The elimination of the 75 per cent category, that is, those who were able to draw 75 per cent of their insurable income on the basis of having five or more children, cost us even more in terms of the effect on the region.
When you take into account the fact that we live in an area which has the distinction of having the lowest per capita income in the country and the highest per capita cost of living, you can understand the hardship members of these two groups suffer. Yet they are the very people who needed protection most-old pensioners and the heads of large families with five or more dependent children.
I am sure hon. members would be interested if I put on record the average per capita incomes of Canadians in the four provinces by comparison with the national average for all Canadians. In my own province, Newfoundland, it is 31 per cent below the national average. In Prince Edward Island it is 31.4 per cent below the national average. In Nova Scotia it is 21 per cent below, and in New Brunswick 23 per cent below. The loss occasioned by this bill is incalculable.
I would remind hon. members that a bulletin released by the Economic Council of the Atlantic Provinces last November had this to say in reference to the loss to the region because of these measures:
The loss in total personal income in the region based on December, 1975 average weekly payments will be nearly $49 million. This is a very sizeable loss to the four provinces, representing approximately one per cent of total provincial personal incomes.
A great deal has been said about the change in the qualifying period from eight to 12 weeks. This, of course, would mean an even heavier additional burden on each of those four provinces at a time when they can ill afford it. It removes from benefit those people who presently qualify under the eight-week provision. More than 7,000 people will be involved in Newfoundland. This will have the effect of seriously exacerbating the unemployment situation in the region because of the loss of cash income circulating in those provinces. It will mean further lay-offs as a result of this loss of income.
I hope these factors will be borne in mind by the minister who sat here all day attentively listening to the debate in his own quiet way. I hope he will take these things into account when the bill gets before the committee. I hope he will take into account the seriousness of the unemployment situation in my own province where the rate is, as I say, about 35 per cent. The hon. gentleman can talk all he likes about Canada Works and Young Canada Works and about his new employment
2664

February 2, 1977
Employment and Immigration
strategy. The fact is, as has already been pointed out, that these programs will be based on statistics supplied by Statistics Canada, which means the awards will be made in my province on the basis of the latest unemployment figures which show a rate of about 14 per cent at a time when the real rate is about 35 per cent.
I am not seeking to criticize or undermine in any way the initiatives already taken. God knows, were it not for the LIP program in the last three years the situation would be even worse than it is. I want to tell the minister I have appreciated the co-operation I have received from him and from his officials, and from the job creation people in his department in my constituency. Under this program we are able to work together to get the best possible use of the dollars spent to
produce jobs. I appreciate his co-operation, and I want to say this to him: do not put too much stress on the Canada Works program because, as the hon. member for Cape Breton has said, this program is merely an extended version of the LIP program, its application on a yearly basis. In other words, instead of a million dollars being concentrated in a short time on the critical months of unemployment, the same amount is now to be stretched out over a one-year period. Nevertheless, without initiatives of this kind, the situation would be so much worse. I shall have more to say about this later. I hope that before long we can get the bill into committee and begin a serious study of its consequences upon the hard hit regions of the country. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question put, pursuant to Standing Order.

Thursday, February 3, 1977
